title: Power Book III: Raising Kanan: Jukebox Cuts Snaps and Pops Water Off in Episode 7 of Season Five
htmlContent:
The episode wastes no time putting Jukebox's suspicions front and center. After the beatdown and betrayal that led to Breeze's firing, Jukebox corners Snaps and Pops with the accusation that has been building for weeks: that they had a hand in Famous's death and lied to keep her in the dark.

The married couple tried to deflect, insisting they barely knew Famous and that whatever the police told her was a distortion. Jukebox isn't buying it. Her line that killers don't get to hide behind fame or family loyalty lands as the episode's thesis: nobody in this circle gets to kill someone connected to the crew and expect business as usual.

What makes the confrontation land is how personal it is. Jukebox isn't approaching this as an outside enforcer; she's treating Snaps and Pops the way you'd treat cousins who broke an unspoken rule. She reminds them, in essence, that the family fed them, protected them, and raised them, and that the debt owed back was basic honesty — something they couldn't manage to give her.

The Side Business That Wasn't Worth It

The heart of the episode's tension is money, specifically, the pills Snaps and Pops have apparently been moving on the side, against a direct order to keep everything legitimate. Jukebox lets them know she's aware of exactly how small the payoff was: enough for a night of drinks, nothing close to what it's costing them now. Her warning about trading a comfortable life for prison food isn't just an insult; it's a reminder that federal exposure changes the math on everyone, and untrustworthy men become liabilities the moment the state comes calling.

When one of them offers to hand over everything made off the pills as a peace offering, Jukebox shuts it down flatly. The damage isn't a debt that can be repaid with the same money that caused it. She tells them plainly that their services are no longer needed and that they're being replaced, effective immediately. The disbelief on their end, the idea that nobody could simply replace them, only underscores how little leverage they actually have left. It's less a firing than an execution of their standing in the organization, even before anything more permanent happens to either of them.

Marvin's Grief and the Need to Feel Something

Away from the business drama, the episode carves out a quieter, heavier detour for Marvin. Visiting Lou's grave, he admits something rare for a man of his temperament: he doesn't know what to do with himself. The admission isn't about strategy or the next move in the street; it's existential. He's not looking for guidance on retaliation or survival — he says outright that he just wants to feel something again, a confession that reads as a man going numb under the weight of everything the family has lost this season.

Raq Seeks Answers From Lou's Psychiatrist

Raq's storyline this episode is about information, or rather, the lack of it. She tracks down Lou's former psychiatrist, hoping to learn what her brother said about her behind closed doors. The psychiatrist won't break confidentiality, even for grief, even for Raq. But the therapist redirects the moment into something sharper: whatever Lou said matters less than what Raq believes about herself. It's a small scene, but it works as commentary on Raq's arc all season; she keeps looking outward for validation or judgment when the real reckoning is internal.

Baptiste's Confession and Collapse

The episode threads back through episode six's pivotal turn, in which Baptiste, wrestling with his conscience, tells Garcia that Snaps and Pops were behind Famous's murder. Baptiste insists he had no idea the killing was coming when the two men first approached him fishing for details about Raq; he frames their fixation on her as something closer to obsession than professional interest. He also flags Garcia as the last officer he trusts to still be clean, a grim acknowledgment of just how compromised everyone else around them has become.

That confession becomes the emotional undertow of the hour. Later, at home, Baptiste puts on his uniform one final time, sits down in his own office, and takes his life. It's a devastating, quiet end for a character who spent his final act trying to do one honest thing before the guilt caught up with him.

Stefano and Breeze Make Their Move on Hafiz

While Raq's world is unraveling from the inside, Stefano and Breeze are working an angle from the outside. The two sit down with Hafiz and pressure him into cutting ties with Raq in favor of a new arrangement with them. When Hafiz raises the obvious problem that Pino won't take the shift well, Stefano brushes off the concern, promising he'll deal with Pino soon enough. It's a small scene, but it signals that the show's power structure is shifting on multiple fronts at once, with Raq's authority under threat both from within her own crew and from rivals circling from outside it.

The Bigger Picture

Taken together, the episode is less about one dramatic set piece and more about accumulated consequence. Snaps and Pops' betrayal, Baptiste's guilt, Marvin's grief, and Stefano's maneuvering all point toward the same idea: the family's grip on its own organization is loosening, and everyone around Raq is being forced to reckon with what loyalty actually costs. By the time the credits roll, Christmas hasn't just been cancelled for Snaps and Pops; it's been cancelled for anyone still hoping this season ends without more blood.
excerpt: In Episode 7 of Season Five of Power Book III: Raising Kanan, Jukebox confronts Snaps and Pops over Famous's death and their unauthorized pill operation, while Baptiste's confession leads to a devastating end and Stefano moves to undercut Raq's empire from the outside.
